meta.description: Not from Thompson's own writing. Bill Murray says it while playing Thompson in the 1980 film Where the Buffalo Roam, which John Kaye scripted.

answer.label: Not Hunter S. Thompson — a line from the film Where the Buffalo Roam
answer.authorDates: b. 1941 · credited screenwriter of Where the Buffalo Roam (1980)
answer.sourceLine: Bill Murray, playing Thompson, says the line in the 1980 Universal film Where the Buffalo Roam. The screenplay is credited to John Kaye, though Kaye has said Thompson and Murray changed parts of the script during filming. No source for the line in Thompson’s own published writing has been identified.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Bill Murray, playing Hunter S. Thompson

source.excerpt: It’s hard to say he got what he deserved, because he never really got anything, at least not in this story. And right now, this story is all we have … It’s sad. But what’s really sad is it never got weird enough for me. I moved to the country when the boat got too crowded.
source.trailTitle: How a movie line became a Thompson quote
trail: 25 April 1980 — Where the Buffalo Roam opens, with Bill Murray as Thompson and a screenplay credited to John Kaye; Thompson’s credit is “executive consultant” (Wikipedia ↗).
14 May 1980 — The Harvard Crimson review ↗ quotes the film’s Thompson as he sighs, “It never got weird enough for me.”
1986–87 — School yearbooks print the line under Thompson’s name with no mention of the film (Academy Herald, 1986 ↗; Selwyn House School, 1987 ↗).
Today — Wikiquote ↗ lists the line with the film’s dialogue, not with Thompson’s own sourced quotations.
source.excerptNote: This transcription is from Wikiquote’s Where the Buffalo Roam page. The same monologue ends “Because it still hasn’t gotten weird enough for me.” The 1980 Harvard Crimson review quotes the line independently.

author.name: John Kaye
author.heading: Who wrote the line
author.bio: John Kaye is the credited screenwriter of Where the Buffalo Roam (1980). His other film credits include American Hot Wax and Rafferty and the Gold Dust Twins, and he later wrote the novels Stars Screaming and The Dead Circus. Credit for this exact line is uncertain: Kaye has said Thompson and Murray changed parts of his script during filming, and the two later added voice-over narration, so no record shows whose hand drafted it.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Thompson
misattribution.intro: The line sounds like Thompson because the character speaking it is Thompson. Bill Murray plays him in a 1980 film. Quoting it without the film turned a scripted movie line into something Thompson supposedly said himself.

items.why: The words are dialogue spoken by Bill Murray as Thompson in Where the Buffalo Roam (1980). The screenplay is credited to John Kaye, and Thompson was credited as “executive consultant” (Wikipedia ↗). Wikiquote’s page of Thompson’s sourced quotations ↗ does not include it.

By the mid-1980s the line was circulating as Thompson’s own. The 1986 Academy Herald yearbook ↗ credits it to “DR. HUNTER S. THOMPSON,” and the 1987 Selwyn House School yearbook ↗ credits it to “Hunter Thompson.”
Aggregators such as Quotewise ↗ and Quotepark ↗ list it under Thompson’s name and show no book, film or interview as its source.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented source is the 1980 Universal film Where the Buffalo Roam ↗, where Bill Murray speaks the line as Thompson. The screenplay is credited to John Kaye, and no source for the line in Thompson’s own published writing has been identified.

context.heading: A line Thompson's own critics picked out
lead: Where the Buffalo Roam is a loose adaptation of Thompson’s early-1970s writing. It is built mainly on his piece about his lawyer friend Oscar Zeta Acosta, who appears in the film as “Carl Lazlo.” Thompson disliked the screenplay. According to Wikipedia ↗, he called it “a bad, dumb, low-level, low-rent script.”

The line still caught on. Reviewing the film for the Harvard Crimson ↗ in May 1980, Jacob V. Lamar wrote that the film’s only insight into Thompson’s character comes when, “reflecting upon his bizarre adventures, he sighs, ‘It never got weird enough for me.’”
context.detailsSummary: Could Thompson have written the line anyway?
detailsBody: Possibly, but no record shows it. Wikipedia reports Kaye’s claim that “Thompson and Murray changed parts of the script during filming,” and that the two “in early 1980 added voice-over narration.” So the film’s final words may not all be Kaye’s. Still, no source assigns this particular sentence to Thompson.
Thompson did write a famous ‘weird’ line: “When the going gets weird, the weird turn pro,” which Wikiquote’s Thompson page ↗ lists. “It never got weird enough for me” is not on that page.
